title: "Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R"

## Repeat a useful workflow

Today you will repeat yesterday's investigation with fewer prompts. Repetition
helps make file handling a tool you can rely on. The biological task remains:
identify the treated samples and prepare a small package that another person
can understand.

We then meet R, which will calculate and plot the measurements. The terminal
and R console are different places to enter instructions; recognising the
difference will prevent a common beginner problem.

## Practical 1: a fresh investigation folder

Return to your shell workspace:

```bash
cd ~/introcomputing-shell
pwd
```

Use commands from the previous lessons to do the following. Read the whole list
once before starting.

1. Create a fresh folder called `day5`.
2. Copy `lab-data.zip` into it and move into `day5`.
3. List the archive's contents without extracting it.
4. Extract it into a folder called `lab-data` inside `day5`.
5. Enter the extracted folder and read the README.
6. Print the treated sample records and save them as `treated-samples.txt`.
7. Count the matching records using a pipe. Explain why the result is two.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Help me get started without doing everything

From the workspace use `mkdir day5`, `cp lab-data.zip day5/`, then `cd day5`.
The slash after `day5/` makes it clear that this destination is a directory.
Use `unzip -l lab-data.zip` before `unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data`.
If a name already exists, inspect it before choosing whether to reuse it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## I cannot remember the search commands

Inside the extracted folder use `grep -F treated samples.tsv`. Add
`> treated-samples.txt` to save the output, or `| wc -l` to count it. Do not
redirect output into `samples.tsv`: that is the original input.
:::

## Practical 2: make a package another person can inspect

Inside the extracted `lab-data` folder, make a folder called `report`. Copy
`treated-samples.txt` into it. Copy `README.txt` into it with the destination
name `context.txt`. These copies keep the original files available.

Through the file manager, add `report/findings.txt` with four short statements:
the number of samples, which received treatment, what the measurements mean,
and what you have **not** yet analysed. For example, identifying a treated
sample does not establish that its treatment changed growth.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Copy and rename commands

```bash
mkdir report
cp treated-samples.txt report/
cp README.txt report/context.txt
```

Create your own findings text in a plain-text editor. Check its saved location
with `ls report` before packaging the folder.
:::

Create and inspect a ZIP package:

```bash
zip -r report-bundle.zip report/
unzip -l report-bundle.zip
unzip report-bundle.zip -d review
ls review/report
```

`zip` creates an archive. `-r` includes the folder's contents recursively,
including any nested folders. `unzip -l` lets you inspect the package, then
extraction into `review` tests what a recipient would receive. You should find
`context.txt`, `findings.txt`, and `treated-samples.txt` inside `review/report`.
Open `findings.txt` from there and check it is readable.

An archive is a snapshot of the files included when it was created or updated.
Editing the ordinary `report/findings.txt` does not automatically update the
ZIP. Make a new clearly named package after making changes. An archive stored
only next to its originals is still vulnerable if the whole computer is lost.

## Practical 3: explain your files to a partner

Take turns. Point to the original archive, extracted source files, selected
records, your findings, and the final report archive. Explain the role of each.
Ask your partner to locate a particular measurement file using the manifest.
Check the path rather than relying on a file that happened to be open already.

If the supported remote environment is ready, repeat just the navigation and
inspection part there. Use the provided transfer route to move a small file,
then identify the local and remote copies. If it is not ready, this step waits;
the local practical still stands on its own.

## Meet R and RStudio

R is a language and computing environment for working with data. RStudio is an
application that provides an editor, an R console, and other tools around R.
The editor holds saved instructions; the console runs them. A terminal is a
shell prompt, not an R console.

Open RStudio using the [R/RStudio setup instructions](../intro/r-rstudio.qmd).
If it is not installed yet, watch the demonstration and use setup support before
week 2. In the **R console**, enter:

```r
44.3 - 25.7
```

R should return `18.6`: the increase in length of plant P01, in millimetres.
The console might print `[1]` before the answer. That marks the position of the
first displayed element; it is not part of the measurement.

Enter this small supplied example in the R console:

```r
initial_mm <- c(25.7, 24.3, 18.0)
final_mm <- c(44.3, 32.3, 32.9)
plot(initial_mm, final_mm,
     xlab = "Initial length (mm)",
     ylab = "Final length (mm)")
```

The `c(...)` pieces collect three values. `<-` gives each collection a name.
`plot(...)` makes a scatter plot: each point is one plant with an initial and
a final length. We will learn these ideas carefully next week; today identify
the axes and check that there are three points. This example includes only
three plants, not the full experiment.

Do not paste `cd`, `grep`, or `unzip` at the R prompt. Likewise, do not paste
R calculations into the Ubuntu shell and expect R to run them automatically.
When a command fails, first identify which program is reading it.

## From a plot to a report

The teacher will show a complete HTML report generated from saved measurements
and an R Markdown file. Notice the biological question, code, figure with units,
and a written interpretation. The goal is to make these together so that the
report can be produced again when new measurements arrive. You will build your
first version next week.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why inspect an archive after making it?

The name of the ZIP does not guarantee what it contains. Listing and extracting
it checks the folder structure and the actual saved files a recipient gets.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Where should `grep` run, and where should `44.3 - 25.7` run?

Use `grep` in the terminal's shell. Enter the calculation in the R console.
The prompt tells you which program is waiting for instructions; learn to check
it before entering a command.
:::

**Save today:** a tested `report-bundle.zip` and the ordinary `report` folder.
Add one sentence to `findings.txt` explaining how the package differs from its
extracted contents. Repackage it if you want that change included in the ZIP.
